power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Borderline personality disorder, a diagnosis that cannot be challenged: If rejecting the diagnosis is a symptom, can the diagnosis ever be wrong? A response to Chazhoor and

author.affiliation:
University of New South Wales
								
									Sydney
									New South Wales
									Australia

text.text: Objective: Chazhoor and Younger describe borderline personality disorder (BPD) as a diagnostic and management challenge in regional inpatient psychiatry, including patients' reluctance to accept the diagnosis and preference for autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) or complex post-traumatic stress disorder (CPTSD).
This Perspective examines the epistemic assumptions embedded in that framing and their implications for trauma, neurodivergence, gender diversity, sensory distress and iatrogenic harm.
Conclusions: Diagnostic disagreement is not evidence for the diagnosis being disputed.

BPD is itself historically and culturally situated, and its application can relocate traumatic, neurodevelopmental, sensory and minority-stress-related distress into a purportedly disordered personality.
When dissent, self advocacy or reports of harm are reinterpreted through the same construct, diagnostic reasoning risks becoming recursive and unfalsifiable.
I argue for moving beyond BPD towards trauma-informed, neurodiversityaffirming, sensory-informed and epistemically just formulations that remain open to revision.

In "Borderline personality disorder: Challenges in an inpatient setting", Chazhoor and   Younger identify genuine problems in regional psychiatry, including scarce specialist psychological services, diagnostic uncertainty and pharmacological over-intervention. 1 However, they also describe hesitance by clinicians and patients to accept BPD as delaying "correct treatment", suggest that symptoms may be attributed to more socially acceptable diagnoses such as CPTSD, ADHD or autism, and link this to social media and a potentially misinformed "self-advocating cohort". 1 Their cited social-media study concerns validation and tensions within ADHD communities; it does not establish that people contesting BPD have incorrectly attributed their experiences to ADHD, autism or CPTSD, nor that BPD is therefore the more accurate explanation. 2 This matters because the disagreement is not occurring between a neutral diagnostic truth and a socially influenced patient narrative.
text.formatted: In "Borderline personality disorder: Challenges in an inpatient setting", Chazhoor and   Younger identify genuine problems in regional psychiatry, including scarce specialist psychological services, diagnostic uncertainty and pharmacological over-intervention. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> However, they also describe hesitance by clinicians and patients to accept BPD as delaying "correct treatment", suggest that symptoms may be attributed to more socially acceptable diagnoses such as CPTSD, ADHD or autism, and link this to social media and a potentially misinformed "self-advocating cohort". <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> Their cited social-media study concerns validation and tensions within ADHD communities; it does not establish that people contesting BPD have incorrectly attributed their experiences to ADHD, autism or CPTSD, nor that BPD is therefore the more accurate explanation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> This matters because the disagreement is not occurring between a neutral diagnostic truth and a socially influenced patient narrative.

text.text: I argue that BPD itself requires equivalent scrutiny.

My position is abolitionist: the problem is not merely that BPD is sometimes applied to the "wrong" person, but that a heterogeneous and value-laden construct continues to translate trauma, neurodivergence, sensory distress, minority stress and relational suffering into pathology of personality. 3, 4 Whose explanatory framework is socially influenced?
text.formatted: My position is abolitionist: the problem is not merely that BPD is sometimes applied to the "wrong" person, but that a heterogeneous and value-laden construct continues to translate trauma, neurodivergence, sensory distress, minority stress and relational suffering into pathology of personality. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4</ref> Whose explanatory framework is socially influenced?

text.text: BPD is historically situated.

Jones traces its development through changing social conditions, psychoanalytic disputes and professional struggles over the boundaries of psychiatry. 5 Tyrer and Mulder similarly question the historical coherence of the category. 6 Immediately before DSM-III, Spitzer, Endicott and Gibbon operationalised competing meanings of "borderline" and argued for separate borderline personality and schizotypal categories. 7 BPD's formal codification was therefore the outcome of contested classificatory work, not the discovery of an ahistorical natural kind.
text.formatted: Jones traces its development through changing social conditions, psychoanalytic disputes and professional struggles over the boundaries of psychiatry. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">5</ref> Tyrer and Mulder similarly question the historical coherence of the category. <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> Immediately before DSM-III, Spitzer, Endicott and Gibbon operationalised competing meanings of "borderline" and argued for separate borderline personality and schizotypal categories. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> BPD's formal codification was therefore the outcome of contested classificatory work, not the discovery of an ahistorical natural kind.

text.text: The epistemic asymmetry becomes more striking when social influence is invoked to discount patients.

Spitzer, a central architect of DSM-III classification, later published work reporting that some gay men and lesbians could change sexual orientation following socalled reparative therapy. 8 The point is not that BPD is invalid simply because of who helped codify it.
text.formatted: Spitzer, a central architect of DSM-III classification, later published work reporting that some gay men and lesbians could change sexual orientation following socalled reparative therapy. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8</ref> The point is not that BPD is invalid simply because of who helped codify it.

text.text: It is that psychiatric authority has never operated outside culture, ideology or prejudice.

Contemporary lived expertise scholarship likewise documents how psychiatric classification has been shaped by racism, sexism, ableism, sanism, homophobia, colonialism and other forms of structural power. 9 Psychiatry therefore cannot reasonably pathologise patients for being influenced by contemporary explanatory frameworks while treating its own diagnostic categories as though they emerged untouched by culture, history, ideology, professional power, prejudice and bigotry.
text.formatted: Contemporary lived expertise scholarship likewise documents how psychiatric classification has been shaped by racism, sexism, ableism, sanism, homophobia, colonialism and other forms of structural power. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> Psychiatry therefore cannot reasonably pathologise patients for being influenced by contemporary explanatory frameworks while treating its own diagnostic categories as though they emerged untouched by culture, history, ideology, professional power, prejudice and bigotry.

text.text: If social influence warrants scrutiny of patient knowledge, epistemic reciprocity requires at least equivalent scrutiny of psychiatric knowledge. 10 From trauma, neurodivergence and minority stress to "personality pathology" More fundamentally, why should recovery from traumatic experiences, particularly childhood abuse, require telling a person that their personality is disordered?
text.formatted: If social influence warrants scrutiny of patient knowledge, epistemic reciprocity requires at least equivalent scrutiny of psychiatric knowledge. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> From trauma, neurodivergence and minority stress to "personality pathology" More fundamentally, why should recovery from traumatic experiences, particularly childhood abuse, require telling a person that their personality is disordered?

text.text: Personalitypathology judgements are not culturally neutral.
They depend on norms concerning appropriate emotional expression, relationality, autonomy, identity and behaviour.
Recasting survival responses to violence as evidence of disordered personality risks relocating the consequences of violence from what happened to the person into who the person supposedly is.

The Royal College of Psychiatrists now explicitly recognises that adult survivors of child sexual abuse can experience iatrogenic harm through misinterpretation, misdiagnosis, disbelief, retraumatisation and diagnostic overshadowing, and recommends trauma-informed, formulation-led care. 11 The same concern applies to neurodivergence.
text.formatted: The Royal College of Psychiatrists now explicitly recognises that adult survivors of child sexual abuse can experience iatrogenic harm through misinterpretation, misdiagnosis, disbelief, retraumatisation and diagnostic overshadowing, and recommends trauma-informed, formulation-led care. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> The same concern applies to neurodivergence.

text.text: Late or unrecognised autism and ADHD are associated with substantial adverse consequences, including poorer mental health. 12 Autistic adults previously labelled with BPD or emotionally unstable personality disorder have described longstanding autistic differences being overlooked, diagnostic overshadowing, stigma, harmful care and difficulty challenging psychiatric interpretations. 13 McQuaid and colleagues similarly show how superficially similar presentations can arise through different mechanisms and emphasise developmental history, camouflaging and gendered diagnostic bias. 14 These findings should not be read as implying that there is a separate population for whom BPD is valid.
text.formatted: Late or unrecognised autism and ADHD are associated with substantial adverse consequences, including poorer mental health. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> Autistic adults previously labelled with BPD or emotionally unstable personality disorder have described longstanding autistic differences being overlooked, diagnostic overshadowing, stigma, harmful care and difficulty challenging psychiatric interpretations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> McQuaid and colleagues similarly show how superficially similar presentations can arise through different mechanisms and emphasise developmental history, camouflaging and gendered diagnostic bias. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> These findings should not be read as implying that there is a separate population for whom BPD is valid.

text.text: From an abolitionist perspective, they illustrate how neurodevelopmental experiences can be absorbed into a personality-pathology framework.
This issue is also intersectional.

Trans and gender diverse (TGD) people show elevated rates of autism, other neurodevelopmental diagnoses and autistic traits. 15 Rodriguez-Seijas and colleagues found that TGD patients had substantially greater odds of receiving BPD diagnoses than cisgender heterosexual patients; the disparity persisted after controlling for purported BPD-specific personality pathology. 16 Porter, Smith and Watts likewise argue that personality-disorder judgements can pathologise responses to gender dysphoria, discrimination and hostile social environments. 17 The risk is cumulative: neurodevelopmental, sensory, trauma-related and minority-stress experiences may all be retranslated as defects of personality.
text.formatted: Trans and gender diverse (TGD) people show elevated rates of autism, other neurodevelopmental diagnoses and autistic traits. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> Rodriguez-Seijas and colleagues found that TGD patients had substantially greater odds of receiving BPD diagnoses than cisgender heterosexual patients; the disparity persisted after controlling for purported BPD-specific personality pathology. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> Porter, Smith and Watts likewise argue that personality-disorder judgements can pathologise responses to gender dysphoria, discrimination and hostile social environments. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> The risk is cumulative: neurodevelopmental, sensory, trauma-related and minority-stress experiences may all be retranslated as defects of personality.

text.text: This is not merely a dispute about labels.

Psychiatric patients are vulnerable to testimonial injustice when their credibility is unjustly reduced because of stereotypes or diagnostic status. 18 Watts applies this directly to BPD, showing how the label can alter how testimony is heard and constrain access to alternative understandings. 19 An umbrella review likewise documents persistent BPD-related stigma across healthcare, diagnostic labelling and institutional structures. 20 The problem becomes recursive when disagreement is interpreted through the diagnosis being disputed.
text.formatted: Psychiatric patients are vulnerable to testimonial injustice when their credibility is unjustly reduced because of stereotypes or diagnostic status. <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> Watts applies this directly to BPD, showing how the label can alter how testimony is heard and constrain access to alternative understandings. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> An umbrella review likewise documents persistent BPD-related stigma across healthcare, diagnostic labelling and institutional structures. <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> The problem becomes recursive when disagreement is interpreted through the diagnosis being disputed.

text.text: Recent work has termed this diagnostic recursivity: self advocacy, reports of iatrogenic harm or resistance to a formulation can be redescribed as "defiance", instability or further evidence of pathology. 3 If accepting BPD is interpreted as insight while rejecting it is attributed to stigma, misinformation, poor insight or the disorder itself, the construct becomes progressively insulated from falsification.
text.formatted: Recent work has termed this diagnostic recursivity: self advocacy, reports of iatrogenic harm or resistance to a formulation can be redescribed as "defiance", instability or further evidence of pathology. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> If accepting BPD is interpreted as insight while rejecting it is attributed to stigma, misinformation, poor insight or the disorder itself, the construct becomes progressively insulated from falsification.

text.text: Questioning whether a stigmatised diagnosis accurately explains one's experiences may instead reflect critical appraisal and epistemic agency.
A patient's preferred explanation is not automatically correct, but neither is the clinician's.
Diagnostic disagreement should trigger scrutiny of the evidence, not become evidence in its own right.
A similar problem appears in interpretations of inpatient behaviour.

Chazhoor and Younger describe extended admission as potentially becoming "maladaptive coping", reluctance to discharge as dependence, and disability support as potentially reinforcing "sick role behaviours". 1 Yet repeated admission, reluctance to leave and requests for support are observable phenomena; "dependency", "maladaptive coping" and "sick role behaviour" are interpretations of their meaning.
text.formatted: Chazhoor and Younger describe extended admission as potentially becoming "maladaptive coping", reluctance to discharge as dependence, and disability support as potentially reinforcing "sick role behaviours". <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> Yet repeated admission, reluctance to leave and requests for support are observable phenomena; "dependency", "maladaptive coping" and "sick role behaviour" are interpretations of their meaning.

text.text: They may instead, or additionally, reflect inadequate community services, trauma, previous harmful discharge, fear, unmet disability needs or an inaccessible environment.

Indeed, Chazhoor and Younger themselves acknowledge long waiting lists and gaps in community-based care. 1 Aves has shown how dependency discourse can legitimise withholding care despite weak evidence that care dependency reflects pathological personality traits. 21 Sensory processing is particularly important.
text.formatted: Indeed, Chazhoor and Younger themselves acknowledge long waiting lists and gaps in community-based care. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> Aves has shown how dependency discourse can legitimise withholding care despite weak evidence that care dependency reflects pathological personality traits. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> Sensory processing is particularly important.

text.text: Autistic inpatients describe stress arising from noise, bright lighting, smells, unpredictability and disrupted routine, with self-harm, aggression or food restriction sometimes occurring in response to overwhelming environments. 22 Such behaviour does not adjudicate between personality pathology and sensory distress.
text.formatted: Autistic inpatients describe stress arising from noise, bright lighting, smells, unpredictability and disrupted routine, with self-harm, aggression or food restriction sometimes occurring in response to overwhelming environments. <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> Such behaviour does not adjudicate between personality pathology and sensory distress.

text.text: The environment may be part of the causal mechanism.

Critical work has described sensory gaslighting, where reports of noise, light or touch as intolerable are reinterpreted as attention seeking, exaggeration or emotional instability rather than investigated as sensory distress. 3 This epistemic problem can continue in psychotherapy.
text.formatted: Critical work has described sensory gaslighting, where reports of noise, light or touch as intolerable are reinterpreted as attention seeking, exaggeration or emotional instability rather than investigated as sensory distress. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3</ref> This epistemic problem can continue in psychotherapy.

text.text: Autistic adolescents in dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) described sensory overload as relevant to self-harm, mixed experiences of validation and invalidation, inaccessible skills and aspects of skills practice that could feel like masking; the authors recommend sensory accommodation, flexibility and neurodiversity-affirming adaptation. 23 Lawson and Farquharson found that clients and staff identified pathologisation and retraumatisation among negative effects of DBT; clients described resistance being categorised as therapy-interfering behaviour and concerns about therapy being reinterpreted as symptoms. 24 Such processes can function as clinical gaslighting when a person's account of sensory suffering or treatment harm is repeatedly displaced by an authoritative interpretation that locates the problem within them.
text.formatted: Autistic adolescents in dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) described sensory overload as relevant to self-harm, mixed experiences of validation and invalidation, inaccessible skills and aspects of skills practice that could feel like masking; the authors recommend sensory accommodation, flexibility and neurodiversity-affirming adaptation. <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> Lawson and Farquharson found that clients and staff identified pathologisation and retraumatisation among negative effects of DBT; clients described resistance being categorised as therapy-interfering behaviour and concerns about therapy being reinterpreted as symptoms. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> Such processes can function as clinical gaslighting when a person's account of sensory suffering or treatment harm is repeatedly displaced by an authoritative interpretation that locates the problem within them.

text.text: The consequences are potentially iatrogenic.

Harmful mental healthcare can itself become a barrier to future care, while mistrust and avoidance may subsequently be interpreted as pathology rather than as responses to prior harm. 25 This creates a self-reinforcing sequence: distress is interpreted through BPD, the person contests the interpretation, the contestation loses credibility because of BPD, and resulting mistrust or escalation is then taken to confirm the original formulation.
text.formatted: Harmful mental healthcare can itself become a barrier to future care, while mistrust and avoidance may subsequently be interpreted as pathology rather than as responses to prior harm. <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> This creates a self-reinforcing sequence: distress is interpreted through BPD, the person contests the interpretation, the contestation loses credibility because of BPD, and resulting mistrust or escalation is then taken to confirm the original formulation.

text.text: This recursive process, and an alternative epistemically just approach, are summarised in Figure 1.
text.formatted: This recursive process, and an alternative epistemically just approach, are summarised in Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>.

text.text: Chazhoor and Younger appropriately recommend longitudinal assessment and caution against prematurely accepting or rejecting diagnoses brought by patients. 1 My concern is that the surrounding framework does not apply equivalent scepticism to BPD itself.
text.formatted: Chazhoor and Younger appropriately recommend longitudinal assessment and caution against prematurely accepting or rejecting diagnoses brought by patients. <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> My concern is that the surrounding framework does not apply equivalent scepticism to BPD itself.

text.text: The alternative is not uncritical acceptance of self-diagnosis, nor simply replacing BPD with autism, ADHD or CPTSD.
It is to stop requiring a characterological construct as the organising explanation for heterogeneous distress.

Clinical reasoning can instead begin with developmental history, trauma, sensory processing, neurodivergence, minority stress, cultural context, material conditions, previous iatrogenic harm and the person's own meaning-making.
Formulations should distinguish observation from inferred motive and remain revisable when evidence changes.

The question should not be how to persuade people to accept that their personality is disordered, but what explanatory framework best supports safety, dignity, understanding and healing without converting disagreement into symptomatology.
BPD should not be afforded epistemic privilege merely because psychiatry has institutionalised it.
Its history, cultural assumptions, stigma and capacity to absorb dissent into its own logic warrant scrutiny.
Diagnostic disagreement is not diagnostic evidence.

I argue that the clinically and ethically safer direction is abolition of BPD as a personalitypathology construct and movement towards trauma-informed, neurodiversity-affirming, sensory-informed and epistemically just formulations in which patient knowledge is neither infallible nor subordinate, and psychiatric interpretations remain accountable, contestable and capable of being wrong.
